**Theorem.** If $g \in L^1(\mathbb{R})$ (Lebesgue integrable), then
$$\lim_{\epsilon \to 0} \int_{\mathbb{R}} |g(x+\epsilon) - g(x)|\,dx = 0.$$

**Proof.**

The key tool is the density of $C_c(\mathbb{R})$ (continuous functions with compact support) in $L^1(\mathbb{R})$: for every $g \in L^1$ and every $\delta > 0$, there exists $h \in C_c(\mathbb{R})$ with
$$\|g - h\|_1 = \int |g(x) - h(x)|\,dx < \delta.$$

Fix $\delta > 0$ and choose such an $h$. Let $\operatorname{supp} h \subseteq [-M, M]$ for some $M > 0$. We use the triangle inequality in the form
$$\|T_\epsilon g - g\|_1 \leq \|T_\epsilon g - T_\epsilon h\|_1 + \|T_\epsilon h - h\|_1 + \|h - g\|_1,$$
where $T_\epsilon f(x) = f(x+\epsilon)$ denotes translation.

**Term 1 and Term 3.** By translation-invariance of Lebesgue measure,
$$\|T_\epsilon g - T_\epsilon h\|_1 = \int |g(x+\epsilon) - h(x+\epsilon)|\,dx = \int |g(y) - h(y)|\,dy = \|g - h\|_1 < \delta.$$
Likewise $\|h - g\|_1 < \delta$. So both the first and third terms are each $< \delta$, independent of $\epsilon$.

**Term 2.** Since $h$ is continuous and supported in $[-M, M]$, it is uniformly continuous. Given $\delta > 0$, there exists $\eta > 0$ such that $|h(y) - h(x)| < \delta$ whenever $|y - x| < \eta$. For $|\epsilon| < \eta$,
$$\|T_\epsilon h - h\|_1 = \int |h(x+\epsilon) - h(x)|\,dx.$$
The integrand is nonzero only when $x + \epsilon \in [-M, M]$ or $x \in [-M, M]$, i.e. on a set of measure at most $2M + |\epsilon| \leq 2M + \eta$. On this set the integrand is $< \delta$ by uniform continuity, so
$$\|T_\epsilon h - h\|_1 < \delta \cdot (2M + \eta).$$
In particular $\|T_\epsilon h - h\|_1 \to 0$ as $\epsilon \to 0$.

**Combining.** For $|\epsilon| < \eta$,
$$\|T_\epsilon g - g\|_1 < \delta + \delta(2M + \eta) + \delta = \delta(2 + 2M + \eta).$$

Since $\delta > 0$ was arbitrary and the right-hand side can be made arbitrarily small (note $M$ and $\eta$ depend on the chosen $h$ and $\delta$, but for each fixed $\delta$ the bound holds for all sufficiently small $\epsilon$), we conclude
$$\lim_{\epsilon \to 0} \int |g(x+\epsilon) - g(x)|\,dx = 0. \qquad \blacksquare$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
